summary:
Flame in Freefall is a bilingual (English/Chinese) interactive web dashboard that helps students, educators, and researchers explore, compare, and interpret NASA International Space Station (ISS) microgravity combustion experiments. 

Using 129 solid-fuel tests from NASA BASS-II (PSI-25) and 274 liquid-droplet tests from NASA FLEX (PSI-69)—alongside 54 ground PMMA tests from the MaCFP database—the dashboard keeps solid and droplet physics strictly separated. It summarizes findings into six live-calculated fire-safety takeaways, explicitly marking each as a NASA measurement or a simplified simulation. Interactive tabs provide a record-level Evidence Explorer, STEM sensitivity curves, a reduced-order 2D buoyancy/diffusion teaching sandbox, and interpretable droplet models (ridge and logistic regression) evaluated using day-grouped cross-validation on unseen test days. 

This student learning tool clarifies how microgravity and cabin airflow change fire behavior, while transparently reporting its scientific limits and non-evaluated targets.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Flame in Freefall turns complex NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) tables into an approachable, verifiable learning dashboard organized into six top-level takeaways and five interactive tabs:

1. Evidence Explorer: Separates solid-material tests (129 BASS-II tests across PMMA shapes/thicknesses, SIBAL fabric, wax, and Nomex) from droplet tests (274 FLEX n-heptane and methanol tests). Every number is computed live from the ingested CSVs, with a Record Inspector linking back to the exact source file, row, and column.

2. STEM Analysis: Interactive parameter sweeps illustrating textbook dimensionless relationships (such as cabin airflow vs. spread proxy and Richardson number regimes) with plain-language physical narration.

3. 2D Physics Sandbox: A reduced-order educational teaching model (explicitly labeled as an illustrative approximation, not a CFD solver) showing how hot gas rises ~56 cm in 1.5 s under Earth gravity (9.81 m/s²) versus spreading sideways with zero rise in orbit (0 m/s²).

4. AI Predictions: Two interpretable scikit-learn models trained on FLEX droplet data—ridge regression for burning-rate constant K (MAE = 0.048 mm²/s, R² = 0.70 ± 0.11 over 255 tests across 80 days, outperforming the 0.109 mm²/s baseline) and logistic regression for early flame-out risk (balanced accuracy = 0.68 ± 0.14 over 204 tests across 73 days vs. 0.50 baseline). It displays input-by-input contributions, retrieves similar NASA runs, and refuses out-of-range inputs. A separate small neural network trained on 54 ground MaCFP PMMA tests is explicitly labeled as a post-test demonstration only, not a space-fire result.

5. Scientific Audit: Reports 25-fold day-grouped cross-validation (5 random splits × 5 folds) to prevent same-day equipment leakage, and honestly marks BASS-II flame-spread speed and extinction as "NOT EVALUATED" because those targets are absent from the PSI-25 table.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Built for STEM students, teachers, and entry-level researchers, the dashboard demystifies counter-intuitive space fire behavior—such as why oxygen enrichment accelerates burning, CO₂ dilution slows it, and airflow replaces buoyancy in orbit—while teaching scientific rigor and data-leakage prevention.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

- Language & Libraries: Python 3.11, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (ridge regression, logistic regression), TensorFlow/Keras (MaCFP ground-test demonstration only), and pytest (5 automated physics sanity checks).

- Verification: Raw NASA CSVs are preserved unchanged and verified against official file sizes, checksums, and NASA/TP-2015-216046 column definitions.

- Deployment: Hosted live on Streamlit Cloud with open-source code on GitHub.

Creativity & Scientific Factors Considered

Rather than forcing incompatible datasets into an unverified "black-box" model, our team prioritized scientific honesty and physical track separation: we avoided pooling solid and liquid fuels, enforced day-grouped validation, labeled every output as measurement vs. model vs. simulation, and avoided overclaiming beyond tested ranges. Disclaimer: This is an educational hackathon prototype, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA, not reviewed by fire-safety experts, and not intended for spacecraft operational decisions.

Super Intelligence (SI) & AI Tool Disclosure (Required Notice)

- Dashboard Models: The live dashboard uses standard machine learning (scikit-learn ridge/logistic regression and a small neural network demo) and does NOT use generative AI inside the app.

- Audio: The demo video narration voice was generated using Microsoft neural text-to-speech (disclosed in the video captions and credits).

- Writing & Coding Assistance: The project report, video script, and selected code refactoring were drafted with assistance from AI tools (Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini); all scientific verification, data checks, and final implementations were reviewed and validated by the team.
